component.name: MeshSat
component.summary: Mesh and satellite gateway in your pocket

description.p: MeshSat keeps people connected when the network is not. On a PinePhone with the Pine64 LoRa back cover it makes the phone a Meshtastic node and runs the MeshSat Bridge beside it: the messages of the LoRa mesh, a RockBLOCK satellite modem on USB, and the MeshSat Hub, routed between each other. This app is MeshSat's own: the screens of MeshSat Android and iOS (Home, Messages, Map, People, Setup), drawn with GTK 4 and libadwaita for a phone in the hand, over the Bridge running on the device.
Pre-release. The radio in the back cover is qualified at 0 dBm only, and a radio that stops answering has to be re-seated by hand; the app says so when it happens.

An SOS takes every route that is set up, as on Android: a leg on a route that is down (a satellite modem not plugged in, a node out of reach, the Hub offline) waits and goes out when the route is back, and the SOS screen says so. The Hub is told over the internet as well. A blank SOS name takes the Hub callsign.

The node's battery with the time it has left, as Android estimates it from the readings the Bridge keeps; Safety and the alarm test's question reach every route that is set up, as Home does; the Hub's password eye as Android draws it.

Closer still to MeshSat Android: the spacing, sizes, chips, rows and colours a side-by-side comparison of every screen found different. The satellite modem of a MeshSat node over Bluetooth: the Satellite page's "Satellite modem on the node" with "Use the node's modem", and the node's health report.

Every screen of MeshSat Android, in its words, proven on the phone. The SOS and the alarm test follow every route through the Bridge's queue, up to "Sent, and the Hub has it" and "Delivered to their phone"; the alarm test's satellite route is a position report to the Hub; an SOS by satellite is no longer held back by the credit budget. The Bridge, the node's API and Meshtastic's web client answer this device only, unless "Share the Bridge on this network" is switched on in Diagnostics. The node page, the notifications, the tray, the quick-settings tile and the lock-screen widget are tested as the rest.

Home as MeshSat Android's: Getting started with Hide, Arrange Home, and the cards for the message queue, the phone's position, the satellite signal and passes, the mobile signal, the satellite mailbox and the recent messages. A welcome at the first start, About, People with your own node, the node banner that says when Bluetooth is off, the Satellite page in Android's words, and a chat's own encryption key. An SOS text to an emergency contact now always goes out as written.

Ham radio, TAK and Reticulum, as MeshSat Android's. APRS through a KISS TNC or directly over APRS-IS, with the passcode worked out from the callsign and a position beacon to APRS-IS only; TAK without a TAK server, to ATAK nearby and to the Hub; Reticulum over TCP, with TLS. The Bridge carries each of them.

The Hub page, as MeshSat Android's: where the link to the Hub stands, in Android's words, with the reason when it fails; Use the Hub; Test the connection; the connection details for setting it up by hand; and the Hub's QR code scanned from the page itself. The Setup row and the Home lane follow the link as the Bridge reports it.

Cards, the QR scanner and the address book, as MeshSat Android's. People you carry: My card, signed by the Bridge, as a QR code with the fingerprint to read aloud; a card scanned with the camera or pasted, checked before it is added; the cards kept on this phone. The scanner uses the phone's camera, or an image. Setup > Messaging scans a kit's key bundle (its key saved the first time, and a changed key asked about), a key, or the Hub's code, which fetches the Hub's settings and applies them; a meshsat://provision link does the same. Emergency contacts can be chosen from the address book.

Zones, offline maps and tracks, as MeshSat Android's. Zones: a long press on the map places a zone, saved in the Bridge, which checks every position a mesh node sends against it and lists who entered or left; the alerts go nowhere else. Offline maps: the built-in world overview, and detailed maps added from MBTiles files, used first and kept when the network is gone; the map says which map it shows. The Map tab draws where each node went in the last 24 hours, lists the nodes with their layers, and People's "Show on map" goes there.

Setup > Messaging as MeshSat Android's: the encryption key of the SMS link (generate, save, copy, paste), encryption on or off, and the automatic decryption of incoming texts, which keeps a text from an ordinary phone as it came; message compression per link where the Bridge can compress; the 30 quick messages. The SMS page takes the number a text with no recipient goes to, or none. Underneath, the Bridge no longer sends a text in the clear on a link set to encrypt when its key cannot encrypt, and checks a key when it is saved.

Mesh radio settings in seven tabs, as MeshSat Android's: the node's name; region (checked against the country the phone is in), preset, transmit power, hops and transmit, each change asked about where Android asks; the channels with what their keys mean, edited without ever touching a key; position sharing; Bluetooth with its pairing modes, asked about before it is switched off; WiFi; setting the clock, restarting, switching off, forgetting heard nodes and a factory reset, each after a question. Only what was changed goes to the node. With the LoRa back cover the transmit power stays at 0 dBm, with the reason beside it. A node over Bluetooth streams its own log to the Node log page while its switch is on.

The rest of Setup > Advanced as native screens in MeshSat Android's words, and the Bridge's web pages gone from the app: the mesh as it was heard, drawn as a graph that lays itself out, with who hears whom and every node; the Bridge's signed audit log with its count, a filter per link, a check of its hash chain and a copy saved where you choose; the certificates and keys the Bridge keeps, imported from a PEM file and deleted after a question; AES-256-GCM by hand with the key the links encrypt with; the links' health and the background service (start after a restart, restart after a question); the node's own log, paused, cleared and saved.

Message queue, Links and Routing rules as native screens, in MeshSat Android's words: the queue with its counts by state, a filter per link, the details of every message and a retry or cancel that is always confirmed; the six Links tabs (a link switched off after a question, reconnected on request, its capabilities, groups, backup links and health); the five Routing rules tabs with the rule editor, the delete that says what it changes, and the queue. The chat's compose bar says how a message goes and what a satellite message costs before it is sent, the bubbles carry a delivery mark and take Android's measures, and All Messages has a search.

Safety as on MeshSat Android: the SOS goes out with your name and position on every route the phone has, the SOS screen shows where it went ("See where it went"), a cancelled SOS tells every route that carried it, and "Test the alarm" sends a test on every route, says it is a test and raises nothing at the Hub. Emergency contacts and the check-in timer in Android's words, with the timer's triggered state. The Bridge underneath carries the SOS words and the Hub's test event.

The foundations under every screen and the faults of 0.5.0 fixed: a text addressed to a node no longer opens the Satellite chat; the lanes no longer keep a modem, a SIM or a Hub while the Bridge is down; opening Safety no longer resets the check-in timer; no call to the Bridge holds the screen; the hold-to-send bar asks first when activated by a screen reader; singular and plural as Android's. An end-to-end test harness runs the app on the phone against a scripted Bridge, and a parity ledger measures the distance to MeshSat Android. An amd64 package for desktops.

MeshSat outside its window: notifications for texts that arrive, messages that did not go and an SOS in progress; the satellite signal as a notification kept up to date; on Phosh a MeshSat tile among the quick settings and a widget on the lock screen; a tray icon where the shell has a tray.

Your node over Bluetooth, as on the other apps: a phone without the LoRa back cover scans for Meshtastic nodes under Setup > Your MeshSat node, pairs with the PIN the node shows, and keeps the node across restarts. The package finds out at boot whether this phone carries the cover and runs the node daemon only then.

The name of a mesh node: "Node !id" until the phone has heard its NodeInfo, as on the other apps; a name heard once is kept across Bridge restarts; a node that has not told its name is asked again on the cadence its firmware accepts. New message lists the nodes heard recently.

SMS as on the other apps: the lane on Home, SMS chats, texts to a number, Setup > SMS, and emergency contacts under Safety who get the SOS by SMS from the phone's own SIM. The Bridge takes the modem from ModemManager; the wordmark is drawn sharp.

Satellite passes as on the other apps: the pass overhead or the next one, the chart of passes against the modem's signal, the surroundings, every pass in the window. The phone's position comes from the system's location service, the node, or a position typed in; the map shows the phone.

The app is MeshSat's own interface now: the Android and iOS apps' screens, colours, type and icons, drawn natively with GTK 4 and libadwaita, with night mode and the map, in place of the Bridge's web console in a web view.
The Bridge binary now carries its web interface (taken from the container image); 0.1.1's showed a blank page.
The app no longer probes the daemon's API port, which threw the Bridge off its session every few seconds.
First package: the node daemon for the LoRa back cover at 0 dBm, its watchdog, the MeshSat Bridge over TCP to the daemon, and this app.
